reply:
HOLD. The technical fact is correct: `latest` does resolve to the most recent published image at pull time. But that's the problem, not the solution.

The cost: **Non-deterministic builds**. Two builds of the same commit on different dates pull different images. In production, this means:
- You can't reproduce a deploy: re-running the same Dockerfile months later pulls a different Node version
- You can't rollback: re-deploying an old commit doesn't actually deploy the old image
- You lose auditability: you don't know what version you're running

On security patches: Pin the *major version*, not a digest. `FROM node:20` gets all 20.x patches automatically but stays deterministic. `FROM node:latest` gets all patches automatically but also gets breaking changes when Node 21 releases.

What would change my mind: evidence that your deployment system re-pulls and re-tests every time anyway, making the non-determinism irrelevant. But standard practice is to build once and promote that image through environments.

grade.note: Correctly clarifies 'latest' resolves at pull time (not always newest by nature of tag), argues for pinning major version for reproducibility, matching ground truth.
